strengths: The paper is built on concrete empirical observations: it quantifies attention recall degradation of existing sparse attention methods on reasoning tasks (Figure 1) and provides visualization-based evidence of spatial locality across attention heads and a stable recency window across decoding steps (Figures 2-3), which directly motivate the design.

The proposed mechanism (Unified Attention Head Selection + Stable Recency Window) is simple, training-free, and clearly formalized in Algorithm 1, and the ablations (Figure 8 for aggregation schemes, Figure 9 for recent-window ratio) are targeted at the two design choices.

The evaluation is relatively thorough for the models tested: four reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), two model sizes, multiple token budgets, comparisons against training-free (Quest, TidalDecode) and training-required (SeerAttention-r) baselines, and an end-to-end system implementation with customized GQA kernels on FlashInfer.

A genuinely interesting finding is that sparse attention errors inflate generation length (Table 1): LessIsMore keeps generation lengths aligned with full attention while baselines generate up to 103% longer sequences, which strengthens the practical significance of improved token selection.
The limitations section is honest and specific, discussing the fixed token budget/ratio, restriction to GQA/TidalDecode pipeline, and the fact that the full KV cache is still maintained in memory.
weaknesses: The generality of the core empirical claims is under-supported. The 'first detailed token-level analysis' is based on a single model (Qwen3-8B), a single layer (Layer 4), and essentially one task (AIME-24) for the qualitative visualizations. Claims that head-specialization assumptions are 'fundamentally challenged' and that the recency window ratio is 'relatively constant' need evidence across models, layers, and tasks.

The central insight (cross-head overlap in important tokens under GQA) is closely related to how GQA already shares KV heads across query heads, and recency windows are well established (StreamingLLM, sliding-window methods). The novelty is thus an incremental combination of known ingredients, and the paper should more carefully delineate the contribution relative to prior work.

Efficiency results are measured on Llama-3.1-8B as a stand-in for the evaluated Qwen3-8B, rather than the model actually used for accuracy. This weakens the link between the accuracy and speed claims and is not fully justified; reported speed-ups are also modest (1.1x decoding, 1.13x end-to-end vs. TidalDecode), so the practical benefit depends on hardware and setup details that are under-specified.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: Quest and SeerAttention-r results are taken from Gao et al. (2025) under their sampling configurations, and those methods apply sparse attention at all layers while LessIsMore/TidalDecode use two full-attention layers; the FairNESS of cross-method accuracy claims (e.g., Figure 6) therefore has caveats the paper should address more explicitly.

Several key ablations rest on very small evidence: Figure 9 appears to be a single AIME-24 problem (the (T)/(F) annotation is per-problem), AIME-24 has only 30 problems, and pass@1 over 16 samples yields wide confidence intervals; the paper reports no error bars or statistical significance despite margins of a few accuracy points in some settings.

Hyperparameters (r=0.25, 4 sink tokens, choice of selection layer) appear tuned per model family, and the paper acknowledges no adaptive budgeting; sensitivity to these choices beyond the single ratio ablation is not explored.

Reproducibility is weakened: the footnote 'Code available at' appears to lack an actual URL in the manuscript, and implementation details of the customized kernels and aggregation (PyTorch primitives) are thin, which matters given that the headline speed-ups depend on system-level engineering.

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and timely problem: existing training-free sparse attention methods degrade accuracy on decode-heavy reasoning workloads due to accumulated selection errors, and the introduction clearly quantifies this (e.g., attention recall dropping to 65–75% on AIME-24 vs. near-perfect recall on retrieval tasks).

The two empirical observations—spatial locality of token importance across attention heads in GQA and a stable recency locality across decoding steps—are clearly presented with visualizations (Figures 2–3) and directly motivate the design, giving the method a principled (if incremental) grounding rather than pure heuristics.

The accuracy evaluation is broad for its scope: two model sizes (Qwen3-8B/4B), four benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), multiple token budgets, and comparisons against both training-free (Quest, TidalDecode) and training-required (SeerAttention-r) baselines, with full numeric tables in the appendix (Tables 2–3).

The generation-length analysis (Table 1) is a valuable and less-common evaluation angle: showing that baselines inflate reasoning length by up to 103% while LessIsMore tracks the full-attention baseline is a meaningful finding about a real failure mode of sparse attention in reasoning.

Ablations are reasonably complete: aggregation scheme comparison (Figure 8), recency window ratio sweep (Figure 9), and selection-layer choice justification (Appendix A.1), and the limitations section is candid about the fixed ratio, TidalDecode dependency, lack of memory savings, and GQA-only scope.
A real systems implementation with customized GQA kernels on FlashInfer and end-to-end latency measurements strengthens the efficiency claims beyond theoretical FLOP counts.
weaknesses: Limited model diversity undermines the generality claims: accuracy is evaluated only on Qwen3-4B/8B (a single model family), and the efficiency evaluation is conducted on Llama-3.1-8B rather than the evaluated models. All conclusions about spatial locality rest on one architecture (GQA, 32 heads) at a single layer (Layer 4); the paper itself concedes extension to MLA/MoE is future work, yet the introduction presents the locality observations as fundamental properties of reasoning.

The observational analysis (Figures 1–3) is based on a single AIME problem and one or few decoding steps, which is thin evidence for claims like 'the first detailed, token-level analysis' and for a fixed 25% recency ratio presented as a general design constant; the ratio ablation (Figure 9) also appears to be run on essentially one problem.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the headline claims: AIME-24/25 contain only 30 problems, and differences such as LessIsMore 75.83 vs. Full Attention 74.48 (and LessIsMore exceeding full attention at K=6000, 76.67 vs. 74.48) are almost certainly within sampling noise, yet are repeatedly cited as accuracy 'preservation or improvement' without confidence intervals, variance across samples, or significance tests.

The technical novelty is modest: the method is a relatively small modification of the TidalDecode pipeline (same two full layers, same selection layers), combining (a) cross-head union/rank aggregation of top-k lists and (b) a fixed-proportion recent-token window. Recency windows are standard (StreamingLLM), and cross-head overlap in GQA is partly structurally expected since heads within a KV group share keys/values. The 1.1× decoding speed-up over full attention and 1.13× end-to-end gain over TidalDecode are practically modest.

Baseline fairness is questionable: Quest and SeerAttention-r are configured with all layers sparse (per Gao et al., 2025) while LessIsMore keeps two full attention layers plus two selection layers, which mechanically advantages LessIsMore in accuracy; the '2× fewer tokens at no accuracy loss' claim should be interpreted with this asymmetry in mind.

No memory-savings benefit: the method retains the full KV cache (acknowledged in Section 5.3), so unlike eviction-based competitors it does not reduce the dominant memory cost for long reasoning; the efficiency contribution is limited to latency.

Reproducibility is weakened by an empty code link (footnote 1 reads 'Code available at' with no URL) and by Figure 7 lacking axis values/legend detail in the reproduction-critical efficiency plot; some notation is also imprecise (e.g., Equation 1's subscript placement, informal definitions of UnionFlatten ranking).

Figure quality undermines the core evidence: Figures 2–3 are qualitative heatmaps from a single layer/problem with small or unlabeled axes, and Figure 9's (T)/(F) annotations, while interesting, constitute anecdotal single-sample evidence for the 25% ratio choice.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it clearly identifies a real problem (sparse attention accuracy degradation on long decode-heavy reasoning generations) and supports the motivation with concrete measurements (Figure 1's attention recall degradation on AIME-24 vs. retrieval tasks).

The two empirical observations (spatial locality of token importance across attention heads in GQA, and a stable recency locality across decoding steps) are interesting, and the method is a direct, faithful implementation of these observations (Unified Attention Head Selection + Stable Recency Window), making the design well-justified rather than ad hoc.

Evaluation covers multiple reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond) at multiple token budgets, with results in appendix tables, and includes both training-free (Quest, TidalDecode) and training-required (SeerAttention-r) baselines.

The efficiency evaluation is more careful than typical: custom GQA kernels on FlashInfer, per-token decoding latency measurements, and an end-to-end analysis (Table 1) that accounts for generation-length inflation—a subtle failure mode of prior sparse methods that the paper quantifies well (30.0K vs. 14.8K tokens for Quest at K=2000).

The ablations are relevant to the core claims: Figure 8 separates the contribution of unified selection under reduced selection frequency (L2 vs. All), and Figure 9 ablates the recency window ratio; the limitations section (Section 5) is honest about fixed hyperparameters, GQA-only scope, and lack of memory savings.

Training-free nature is a practical advantage over retraining-based approaches like SeerAttention-r, and the observed generation-length reduction (7% shorter than TidalDecode) is a valuable secondary effect.
weaknesses: Limited generality of evidence: all accuracy results use only Qwen3-4B/8B, two models from the same family that both use GQA. The central claim that per-head specialized selection is a 'local optimum' contradicts prior work (DuoAttention, TidalDecode), but the supporting evidence (Figures 2-3) consists of visualizations from a single layer (Layer 4), a single problem, and a few decoding steps. No quantitative overlap statistics, no analysis across layers/models/tasks are provided, so the 'first detailed token-level analysis' claim is under-supported.

Statistical rigor is weak for the headline accuracy claims. AIME-24/25 have only 30 problems; differences such as 75.83 vs. 74.48 (LessIsMore vs. Full Attention) or 73.75 vs. 71.35 (vs. SeerAttention-r) at K=4000 are within plausible sampling noise with 16 samples, yet no confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests are reported. The 'matches or improves accuracy' claim rests on such margins.

The Figure 9 ablation annotates correctness ('T'/'F') from what appears to be a single run of a single AIME problem, which is far too fragile to validate the 25% recency window design choice; a sweep over problems with pass@k statistics would be needed.

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: Quest and SeerAttention-r results are taken from a prior paper's configurations (all layers sparse, block size 64), while LessIsMore and TidalDecode use a custom pipeline with full-attention layers and tuned selection layers; the comparison in Figure 6/Table 1 may therefore mix incompatible sparsity configurations.

The efficiency evaluation is conducted on Llama-3.1-8B rather than the evaluated reasoning models, and on a single RTX A5000 GPU; the headline 1.1x decoding and 1.13x end-to-end speedups are modest and hardware/batch-size specific, with no batching or memory-footprint analysis (acknowledged in Section 5.3, but the title-level 'efficiency' claim is accordingly narrow).

Attention recall itself is imperfect under the proposed scheme: Figure 8 shows LessIsMore(L2) recall degrading to ~0.84 at 20K tokens, so the claim of generalization across layers is only partially supported; the reasoning for why degraded recall nonetheless yields lossless accuracy is not analyzed.

The 'Code available at' footnote is empty in the manuscript, which hurts reproducibility; reproducibility also depends on unstated details (e.g., exact kernel implementations, prompt formats, sampling temperatures for baselines).

The technical novelty is incremental: cross-head token aggregation is a natural simplification given GQA (KV heads are already shared), and a recency window is standard (StreamingLLM); the contribution is primarily an empirical insight plus system integration rather than a new mechanism.

strengths: The paper makes a well-motivated empirical observation (cross-head spatial locality and stable temporal recency of token importance in reasoning attention) and derives the method design directly from it, with ablations (Figures 4, 7, 8) that specifically validate unified selection over head-local and randomized selection under infrequent re-selection.

Evaluation is fairly broad: four reasoning models (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B) across AIME-24/25, MATH500, and GPQA-Diamond, plus long-context generalization (NiTH, LongBench, MHA-based LongChat), with multiple sampled traces per problem.

The analysis of generation-length inflation in prior sparse methods (Table 2) is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution, and LessIsMore's preserved reasoning lengths are a practically meaningful advantage beyond raw accuracy.

Efficiency evaluation is reasonably thorough, including kernel-level FLOP/memory-transfer/latency profiling (Table 4) and end-to-end integration in SGLang with FlashInfer, with the fair choice of identical re-selection layers for LessIsMore and TidalDecode.
The method is training-free and architecture-agnostic (GQA and MHA), which improves its practical usefulness.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core mechanism is largely TidalDecode with two changes—aggregating per-head top-k lists into a unified cross-head ranking, and reserving a fixed fraction r of the budget for recent tokens. Both ideas individually exist in prior work (cross-head sharing in NSA-related designs, sliding/recency windows in StreamingLLM), so the contribution is primarily a recombination guided by a new observation.

The headline 'lossless accuracy' claim rests heavily on AIME-24/25, which contain only 30 problems. With 64 samples the standard error of Pass@1 is roughly ±1.7 points, so several reported 'improvements over full attention' (e.g., 75.56 vs 74.48) are within noise. No confidence intervals, paired tests, or variance analysis are provided.

Internal inconsistencies and overstatements: the abstract claims 'up to 1.6x end-to-end speedup' while Figure 6a reports 1.55x/1.58x; the '1.72x faster sparse attention' is relative to TidalDecode rather than full attention, which could mislead; Table 2 shows LessIsMore itself inflates generation length at K=2000 (15.8K vs 14.8K), slightly contradicting the 'nearly identical' claim.

The cross-head locality claim, which is the paper's central insight, is quantitatively under-supported: evidence is mostly qualitative heatmaps (Figures 2, 9, 10) on one model (Qwen3-8B, mainly Layer 4). No overlap statistic (e.g., mean top-k Jaccard or ranking correlation) across heads, layers, and models is reported.

As a selection-based method, the full KV cache is retained; the paper does not clearly discuss that the benefit is compute/latency only, not memory, which is a significant caveat for the deployment context it emphasizes.

Some design elements appear heuristic despite claims of being 'direct consequences' of the observations: the choice of two full-attention layers and one selection layer, the number of re-selection layers, and the r=0.25 window ratio (the ablation in A.1.2 is single-task and single-problem-scale, and 50%/75% windows also succeed, so why exactly 25% is optimal is not explained).

Generality of the observation across model families and, importantly, across reasoning vs. non-reasoning models is not established: no comparison of cross-head overlap between reasoning and standard LLMs, so it remains unclear whether the effect is special to RL-trained reasoning models or a general property.

The recall-vs-accuracy argument is correlational; the paper would benefit from more direct evidence linking recall degradation to specific reasoning failures, beyond indirect generation-length inflation.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is blank, some citations are malformed (e.g., duplicated H2O entries, 'AI, 2024b' used for both Meta Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek references in Section 4.3), and the 'UnionFlatten' ranking/aggregation procedure is under-specified for reproducibility (how head rankings are combined and ties broken).

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: decoding-time attention is a genuine bottleneck for long-horizon reasoning, and the observation that existing sparse attention methods degrade on reasoning workloads (Figure 1) is convincingly demonstrated.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: four reasoning models across two families (GQA and MHA), four reasoning benchmarks with multi-sample Pass@1 (64 traces for AIME, 16 for GPQA), plus long-context generalization via Needle-in-the-Haystack (up to 100K context) and LongBench (Tables 7-9).

Baselines are treated fairly and carefully: the same re-selection layer selection procedure is used for both LessIsMore and TidalDecode (Section A.5, Table 11), strong baselines include both training-free (Quest, TidalDecode, StreamingLLM) and training-required (SeerAttention-r) methods.

The design choices are tied to empirical analysis rather than heuristics: the ablations in Section A.1 (aggregation strategy, recency window ratio r, L2 vs. all-layer selection in Figures 4 and 7) directly validate the cross-head unified selection and proportional recency window.

The efficiency evaluation is thorough for a systems contribution: kernel-level FLOP/memory-transfer/latency profiling (Table 4), integration into a real serving stack (SGLang + FlashInfer, Table 3), and an interesting finding that unified selection avoids generation-length inflation (Table 2), which compounds the effective speedup.
Code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The core mechanism is a combination of known ingredients: cross-head aggregation of top-k scores, a recency window (essentially StreamingLLM's sliding window made proportional), and infrequent re-selection with index reuse (directly inherited from TidalDecode, on which the method is explicitly instantiated). The contribution is closer to a well-executed refinement of TidalDecode than a new mechanism.

The central empirical claim—cross-head spatial locality in reasoning attention—rests on visual evidence (Figures 2, 9, 10) from essentially one model (Qwen3-8B) at one layer (Layer 4) and a handful of decoding steps. No quantitative overlap statistics, no coverage of other layers/models beyond qualitative assertions, and no discussion of when the assumption would fail. Given that the entire method hinges on this claim, the analysis depth is insufficient.

Statistical rigor is lacking. On 30-problem AIME sets, Pass@1 differences of 1-2 points (e.g., LessIsMore 73.8 vs. Full Attention 74.5 at K=2000 in Table 2, or several 'bold' improvements in Tables 5-6) are well within sampling noise, yet the paper repeatedly claims 'matches or exceeds' and 'lossless' accuracy. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

The headline claim of 'up to 87.5% sparsity on AIME-24 with no accuracy loss' overstates: at the smallest budget (2K, ~87.5% sparsity) accuracy is actually slightly below full attention for Qwen3-8B (73.8 vs. 74.5) and DeepSeek-8B (43.2 vs. 44.2), and the abstract's framing glosses over this.

Some methods details are under-specified or inconsistent: the 'UnionFlatten' aggregation and ranking procedure is not precisely defined (how are ties and per-head multiplicities ranked?), the number of reserved 'attention sink' tokens interacts with the budget in unstated ways, and there are numerous typos/editorial errors (e.g., 'Qwen3-4' model name, odd cross-references like '(Figures 1a and 5)', 'Section 2.3 visualizes' self-reference, 'Dimond').

The recency locality observation is largely a confirmation of known behavior (StreamingLLM, attention sinks literature); the paper's framing presents it as a discovery about reasoning models, but the distinction from standard generation is asserted rather than rigorously contrasted (Figure 1b compares only retrieval vs. reasoning under one method).

Efficiency gains are moderate: 1.6x end-to-end speedup is only realized at 64K context with a 2K budget on an 8B model; at 16K the speedup is ~1.1x, and there is no evaluation on larger models or batched serving regimes where the recency-window and selection overheads could matter more.

The limitations discussion is thin: no discussion of applicability to models with different attention architectures (e.g., sliding-window layers, MoE), sensitivity of results to the single hard-coded r=0.25 across all tasks, or failure cases where unified selection would discard head-specific but critical tokens.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: sparse attention methods that work on retrieval-style long-context tasks degrade on long-horizon reasoning. The observation-driven framing (attention recall as a diagnostic, cross-head spatial locality, temporal recency locality) is well motivated and clearly presented.

Evaluation breadth is a decisive strength: four models across two families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B), multiple reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), with reasonable sample counts (64 traces for AIME), plus long-context generalization results (NiTH at 10K–100K, LongBench, MHA-based LongChat) in the appendix.

The generation-length inflation analysis (Table 2) is a genuinely interesting finding—sparse methods like Quest generate up to 103% longer traces at low budgets—showing that accuracy metrics alone understate the cost of selection errors, and LessIsMore avoids this failure mode.

Kernel-level analysis is substantive: end-to-end TBT speedups in both a custom stack (up to ~1.58x) and SGLang/FlashInfer (up to 1.51x), plus FLOP/memory-transfer/latency profiling (Table 4) that explains why unified selection helps GQA models (reduced redundant KV loading per KV group).

Ablations are reasonably thorough: aggregation strategy (Figure 7), recency-window ratio r (Figure 8), re-selection layer choice (Table 11), and CUSA layer placement; design choices are tied back to the observed locality structures rather than presented as pure heuristics.
Code is released and hyperparameters (r=0.25, attention sinks, layer selections) are documented, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The core mechanism—unified token selection across heads plus a recency window, instantiated on top of TidalDecode—is an incremental refinement of prior selection-based methods. In GQA models, heads within a KV group already share keys/values, so cross-head sharing is partially built into the architecture; the 'Randomized Top-k' baseline itself shows a single head's selection transfers well, which weakens the framing of cross-head unification as a key discovery. The central 'global importance' insight is asserted more than rigorously established beyond qualitative heatmaps (Figures 2, 9, 10).

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the headline 'matches or exceeds full attention' claim. AIME has only 30 problems; a 1–2 point Pass@1 difference (e.g., 73.00 vs 74.48 at K=2K on AIME-24, or several MATH500/GPQA entries below Full Attention) is well within sampling noise, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Tables 5–6 omit all sparse baselines, making the 'always outperforms all others' claim in Figure 5 hard to verify numerically.

Some experimental inconsistencies: Table 2 uses 16 samples per problem while the main results use 64; the recency ratio r=0.25 is validated on a single AIME problem (Figure 8); and re-selection layers are tuned via a needle-in-a-haystack procedure, which may favor retrieval behavior over reasoning behavior—the generalization of this tuning to reasoning is asserted but not directly validated.

Efficiency gains are modest and hardware-dependent: ~1.1x at 16K context only becomes meaningful (1.5–1.6x) at 64K, and evaluations use an 8B model on a single GPU; no results on larger models, MLA architectures (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 style), or batched/contended serving scenarios where KV loading dynamics differ.

The claim that 'token importance is global' partially contradicts well-established head-specialization findings, and the paper's resolution (reasoning workloads differ) is supported mainly by single-layer (Layer 4) visualizations on selected problems rather than quantitative overlap statistics across layers and models.

There is no explicit limitations section; risks such as dependence on the accuracy of the selection layer, behavior on tasks where heads are genuinely specialized, or applicability to non-English/reasoning-distilled models are not discussed.
Minor presentation issues: abstract claims 'up to 1.6x' while Figure 6a reports 1.58x; inconsistent naming of speedups across sections; Figure 8's legend and annotation are hard to parse.
